q: These fatty acids all have 18 carbons. Which has the lowest melting point?
h: Each cis double bond puts a kink in the chain. How do kinks affect packing?
w: More cis kinks mean poorer packing and weaker dispersion forces, so linolenic acid melts lowest (about −11 °C). Saturated stearic acid packs best and melts highest; this is why oils are liquid and butter is solid.

q: Linolenic acid is an omega-3 fatty acid. “Omega-3” means that
c: the first double bond is 3 carbons from the methyl (CH<sub>3</sub>) end
the first double bond is at carbon 3 from the –COOH end
it has 3 carbons fewer than stearic acid
h: Omega (ω) is the last letter of the Greek alphabet, so count from the opposite end of the chain.
w: Omega numbering counts from the CH3 (omega) end: the first C=C starts at carbon 3 from that end. Linolenic acid happens to have three double bonds too, but that is not what ω-3 means.

q: A triacylglycerol (triglyceride) is formed from
c: glycerol and three fatty acids joined by ester bonds
glycerol and three fatty acids joined by amide bonds
sphingosine, a fatty acid and phosphate
h: Fatty acids are carboxylic acids and glycerol has three –OH groups. What bond do acids and alcohols form?
w: Each –OH of glycerol forms an ester with a fatty acid: glycerol + 3 fatty acids. Sphingosine is the backbone of sphingolipids.

q: How many moles of NaOH are needed to completely saponify 1 mole of a triacylglycerol?
h: Count the ester bonds; each one uses one hydroxide.
w: A triacylglycerol has three ester bonds, so 3 mol NaOH give glycerol and three moles of sodium fatty-acid salts (soap).

q: A triacylglycerol contains one oleic acid (1 C=C) and two linoleic acids (2 C=C each). How many moles of H<sub>2</sub> are needed to fully hydrogenate 1 mole of it?
h: Each C=C uses one H<sub>2</sub>. Add up the double bonds in all three chains.
w: 1 + 2 + 2 = 5 mol H2. Answering 3 counts the fatty acids instead of the double bonds. The ester C=O groups are not hydrogenated.

q: Beeswax and carnauba wax (used in dental impression materials and car polish) are
c: esters of a long-chain fatty acid and a long-chain alcohol
triacylglycerols made only from saturated fatty acids
steroids built from four fused carbon rings
phospholipids with a choline head group
h: Waxes have only one ester bond. What is on each side of it?
w: A wax is one ester made from a long-chain fatty acid and a long-chain alcohol, which makes it very water-repellent. Triacylglycerols contain glycerol.

q: Lecithin, a glycerophospholipid, contains glycerol, two fatty acids, a phosphate group and
h: Glycerophospholipids have a polar head made of phosphate plus a small nitrogen-containing alcohol.
w: Lecithin = phosphatidylcholine: glycerol + 2 fatty acids + phosphate + choline. A third fatty acid would make a triacylglycerol.

q: Sphingomyelin, abundant in the myelin sheath around nerve cells, differs from glycerophospholipids because its backbone is
h: The name of the lipid class tells you its backbone.
w: Sphingolipids are built on sphingosine; its amino group forms an amide with one fatty acid. Glycerophospholipids are built on glycerol.

q: Cholesterol, the sex hormones and cortisone are steroids. All steroids contain
c: three fatty acids bonded to a glycerol backbone
a long-chain fatty acid joined by an ester bond
a phosphate head group and two fatty-acid tails
h: Steroids are lipids with no fatty acids; recognize them by their ring system.
w: The steroid nucleus is four fused rings: three cyclohexane rings and one cyclopentane ring. Cholesterol adds an –OH and a hydrocarbon side chain.

q: In the fluid-mosaic model of a cell membrane, the phospholipid bilayer is arranged with
c: polar heads facing the water and nonpolar tails inside
nonpolar tails facing the water and polar heads inside
all molecules lying flat on the cell surface
h: Like dissolves like: which part of a phospholipid should touch water?
w: The hydrophilic heads face the watery inside and outside of the cell while the hydrophobic fatty-acid tails point toward each other in the middle. Proteins float in this layer, like a mosaic.

q: Aspirin and ibuprofen reduce pain and inflammation by blocking the COX enzyme, which converts arachidonic acid (a 20-carbon fatty acid) into a family of eicosanoids. Which lipids do these drugs keep the body from making?
c: prostaglandins, which contain a five-membered ring
steroids, which contain four fused rings
triacylglycerols, which contain three ester bonds
sphingolipids, which contain a sphingosine backbone
h: “Eicosa-” means 20. Which choice is an eicosanoid made from a 20-carbon fatty acid?
w: COX converts arachidonic acid into prostaglandins, the eicosanoids that cause pain, fever and inflammation; blocking COX is how NSAIDs work. Steroids are made from cholesterol, and triacylglycerols and sphingolipids are not eicosanoids.

q: Partial hydrogenation of vegetable oils is a health concern mainly because it
c: converts some cis double bonds to trans
adds cholesterol to the vegetable oil
breaks the ester bonds to glycerol
makes the fatty acids more unsaturated
h: During partial hydrogenation, some double bonds remain but change shape.
w: Some remaining double bonds isomerize to the trans form; trans fats raise LDL cholesterol and the risk of heart disease. Hydrogenation makes fats less, not more, unsaturated, and plant oils contain no cholesterol.

q: LDL carries cholesterol from the liver out to the tissues, where excess can deposit in artery walls. HDL is often called “good cholesterol” because it
c: carries cholesterol from the tissues back to the liver
carries cholesterol from the liver out to the tissues
carries more triacylglycerol than any other lipoprotein
carries only phospholipid and protein, with no cholesterol
h: Think about the direction of transport. Which direction lowers the cholesterol that can deposit in artery walls?
w: HDL picks up excess cholesterol from tissues and returns it to the liver, where it can be made into bile salts and removed. LDL delivers cholesterol to tissues, and high LDL leads to plaque (atherosclerosis). Chylomicrons carry the most triacylglycerol.

q: Linoleic acid and linolenic acid are called essential fatty acids because
c: the body cannot make them, so they must come from the diet
they are the only fatty acids found in cell membranes
they are saturated and provide the most energy per gram
the body makes them from glucose when the diet lacks fat
h: “Essential” in nutrition means the same thing here as it does for essential amino acids.
w: Humans cannot put double bonds at the omega-3 and omega-6 positions, so these polyunsaturated fatty acids must be obtained from food. They are unsaturated, not saturated.

q: Butter and lard are solids at room temperature, while olive oil is a liquid. The best explanation is that the animal fats contain more
c: saturated fatty acids, whose straight chains pack closely
unsaturated fatty acids, whose cis kinks pack closely
glycerol per molecule, which raises the melting point
short-chain fatty acids, which form hydrogen bonds
h: Compare the shapes of saturated chains and cis-unsaturated chains. Which shape lets molecules pack tightly?
w: Saturated chains are straight and pack closely, giving stronger dispersion forces and higher melting points. Cis double bonds put kinks in the chains, so oils (mostly unsaturated) pack poorly and stay liquid. Every triacylglycerol has exactly one glycerol.

q: Glucose moves into red blood cells from higher to lower concentration through a specific membrane protein, without using ATP. This is
h: Ask two questions: does it use energy, and does it need a protein?
w: Movement down a concentration gradient with no energy input is passive; because it needs a protein carrier it is facilitated transport. Simple diffusion needs no protein (small nonpolar molecules such as O2), and active transport uses ATP to move against a gradient.

q: Which lipid does NOT undergo saponification with NaOH?
h: Saponification is the hydrolysis of an ester bond by a base. Which lipid has no ester group?
w: Waxes, glycerophospholipids such as lecithin, and triacylglycerols all contain ester bonds that NaOH hydrolyzes. Cholesterol is a steroid alcohol with no ester group, so it is nonsaponifiable.

q: Which biomolecule contains ester linkages as its key functional group?
h: An ester is –COO– joining an acid to an alcohol. Which molecule is made from glycerol plus fatty acids?
w: A triacylglycerol is glycerol esterified with three fatty acids (three ester bonds). Amylose has acetal (glycosidic) links, a tripeptide has amide (peptide) bonds, and cholesterol is a steroid alcohol with no ester.

q: During β-oxidation, a fatty acyl chain is oxidized at its β carbon. Counting the carboxyl carbon as C1, which carbon is the β carbon?
c: C3, two carbons away from the carboxyl carbon
C2, the carbon right next to the carboxyl carbon
the CH<sub>3</sub> carbon at the far end of the chain
h: Greek letters start with the carbon attached to the carboxyl carbon: α first, then β.
w: The α carbon is C2 (attached to the carboxyl carbon) and the β carbon is C3. The CH3 carbon at the far end is the ω (omega) carbon, used to name omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acids.

q: An 18-carbon fatty acid has one double bond, between C9 and C10 (counting the carboxyl carbon as C1). How is it classified?
h: The omega number counts from the CH<sub>3</sub> end (the ω carbon is ω1) to the first carbon of the double bond.
w: The ω carbon is C18 (ω1), so C10 is 18 − 10 + 1 = ω9. The double bond starts 9 carbons from the methyl end: omega-9 (this is oleic acid in olive oil). Omega-10 comes from counting to C9 instead.

q: Testosterone, estradiol, cortisol and aldosterone are hormones made in the body from which lipid?
h: These hormones all share the same four-fused-ring skeleton. Which lipid has that skeleton?
w: These are steroid hormones; their four fused rings come from cholesterol. Arachidonic acid is the starting material for eicosanoids (prostaglandins), not steroids.

q: Which structural description fits a prostaglandin, an eicosanoid that causes inflammation?
c: a 20-carbon fatty acid with a five-membered carbon ring
four fused carbon rings with an –OH group on the first ring
glycerol joined to three long fatty acid chains by ester bonds
sphingosine bonded to a fatty acid, phosphate and choline
h: “Eicosa-” means 20. Eicosanoids are made from a 20-carbon fatty acid.
w: Prostaglandins are made from arachidonic acid (20 C) and contain a five-membered ring within the 20-carbon fatty acid chain. Four fused rings describes a steroid; glycerol + 3 fatty acids is a triacylglycerol; the last choice is sphingomyelin.

q: A triacylglycerol is heated with water and a strong acid catalyst (acid hydrolysis). What are the products?
c: glycerol and three fatty acid salts (soap)
three glycerol molecules and one fatty acid
one fatty acid and a diacylglycerol ester
h: Hydrolysis breaks each ester bond. Is a strong base present to turn the acids into carboxylate salts?
w: Acid hydrolysis breaks all three ester bonds, giving glycerol and three free fatty acids. Base hydrolysis (saponification with NaOH) gives glycerol and three fatty acid salts, which are soaps.

q: Which substance crosses a cell membrane mainly by simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer?
h: The bilayer interior is nonpolar. Which molecules can slip through without a protein channel or carrier?
w: Small, nonpolar or uncharged molecules such as O2, CO2 and (to some extent) H2O diffuse directly through the bilayer. Glucose needs a carrier protein (facilitated transport), and charged ions need channels or pumps.

q: Nerve cells use the Na<sup>+</sup>/K<sup>+</sup> pump, which uses ATP to move 3 Na<sup>+</sup> out and 2 K<sup>+</sup> in, both from lower to higher concentration. This is an example of
h: Look at the direction (with or against the gradient) and whether ATP energy is spent.
w: Moving ions against their concentration gradients requires energy from ATP: active transport. Facilitated transport also uses a protein, but moves solutes from higher to lower concentration with no ATP.

q: After fat digestion, triacylglycerols are re-formed inside intestinal cells. How are they transported away from the intestine?
c: Packaged into chylomicrons that enter the lymph
Dissolved directly in the blood plasma
Bound to hemoglobin in red blood cells
Converted to glucose before entering the blood
h: Triacylglycerols are nonpolar and do not dissolve in water. They need a coat of protein and phospholipid.
w: Triacylglycerols are coated with proteins and phospholipids to form chylomicrons, lipoproteins that enter the lymph and then the bloodstream. Fats are too nonpolar to dissolve in plasma, and hemoglobin carries O2, not lipids.

q: Gram for gram, fat stores provide more than twice as much energy as glycogen. Which is the best explanation?
c: Fatty acid carbons are more reduced, so oxidizing them yields more NADH and FADH<sub>2</sub>.
Fatty acids have more oxygen atoms per carbon, so they release more energy when oxidized.
Fats skip the citric acid cycle and electron transport, so less energy is lost as heat.
Fats are stored with extra water, and that water adds to the energy they release.
h: Compare a –CH<sub>2</sub>– group in a fatty acid with an H–C–OH group in glucose. Which one can still be oxidized more?
w: The –CH2– carbons of fatty acids are highly reduced, so oxidizing them yields more reduced coenzymes and more ATP per gram (about 9 vs 4 kcal g⁻¹). Glucose carbons already carry O. Fat is also stored nearly water-free, while glycogen holds water, which adds mass but no energy.

q: Palmitoleic acid, found in macadamia nut oil, is CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>5</sub>CH=CH(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>7</sub>COOH. Counting from the methyl (omega) end, which type of fatty acid is it?
h: Make the CH<sub>3</sub> carbon number 1 and count toward the C=C. The omega number is the first carbon of the double bond.
w: CH3 is ω1, the five CH2 groups are ω2–ω6, so the double bond starts at ω7: an omega-7 fatty acid. Counting from the –COOH end puts the double bond at C9, which is the tempting omega-9 mistake.

q: Rank by chain length: lauric, myristic, palmitic and stearic acids are saturated and occur in animal fats. Which one stays solid to the highest temperature?
h: For saturated fatty acids, how does chain length affect the dispersion forces between chains?
w: Longer saturated chains have more surface contact and stronger dispersion forces, so they melt at higher temperatures. The 18-carbon stearic acid melts highest.

q: Elaidic acid is the trans isomer of oleic acid (an 18-carbon acid with one cis double bond). Elaidic acid melts at a much higher temperature than oleic acid. Why?
c: The trans chains are nearly straight and pack closely.
The trans double bond adds hydrogen bonds between chains.
Elaidic acid has fewer carbon atoms than oleic acid has.
The trans double bond puts a sharper kink in each chain.
h: Picture the chain shape around a cis double bond and around a trans double bond. Which shape stacks better?
w: A cis double bond puts a kink in the chain that keeps chains apart. A trans double bond leaves the chain nearly straight, so the chains pack closely, raising the melting point, which is why trans fats behave like saturated fats.

q: A soap maker heats glyceryl tripalmitate (a triacylglycerol made from three palmitic acids) with aqueous KOH. What are the products?
c: three glycerol and one potassium palmitate
h: This is saponification (base hydrolysis). Each ester bond breaks, and in base the fatty acids end up as their salts.
w: Base breaks all three ester bonds, giving glycerol and three potassium palmitate (soap). Free palmitic acid forms only in acid hydrolysis; in KOH the acid is deprotonated to its K+ salt.

q: A soap maker converts 0.250 mol of olive-oil triacylglycerol into soap. What mass of sodium hydroxide (40.00 g mol⁻¹) does the reaction consume?
h: A triacylglycerol has three ester bonds. How many NaOH does each molecule need?
w: Each triacylglycerol needs 3 NaOH: 0.250 mol × 3 = 0.750 mol NaOH × 40.00 g mol⁻¹ = 30.0 g. Using a 1 : 1 ratio gives 10.0 g.

q: A lipid from brain tissue is hydrolyzed. The products are sphingosine, one fatty acid and galactose; no phosphate or glycerol is found. What type of lipid is it?
h: Look at the backbone (sphingosine or glycerol) and whether the head group is a phosphate or a sugar.
w: A sphingosine backbone with a monosaccharide head group and no phosphate is a glycolipid (cerebroside). Sphingomyelin also has sphingosine but carries a phosphate–choline head group.

q: Which lipoprotein carries cholesterol from the liver to the body's tissues, and is linked to plaque buildup in arteries when its level is high?
h: One lipoprotein delivers cholesterol out to cells; another brings excess cholesterol back to the liver.
w: LDL (low-density lipoprotein) delivers cholesterol to cells; when it is high, cholesterol deposits in artery walls. HDL does the opposite, returning cholesterol to the liver.

q: A nutrition label separates fats into saturated, monounsaturated and polyunsaturated. Which of these fatty acids belongs in the polyunsaturated group?
c: linoleic acid, with two C=C bonds
oleic acid, with one C=C bond
stearic acid, with no C=C bonds
palmitic acid, with no C=C bonds
h: 'Poly' means more than one. Count the carbon–carbon double bonds.
w: A polyunsaturated fatty acid has two or more C=C bonds, so linoleic acid fits. Oleic acid, with one C=C, is monounsaturated; stearic and palmitic acids are saturated.

q: Triolein, a liquid oil, contains three oleic acids (18 carbons, one cis C=C each). It is completely hydrogenated with H<sub>2</sub> and a Ni catalyst. What is the product?
h: Hydrogenation adds H<sub>2</sub> across each C=C without changing the number of carbons. Which saturated 18-carbon acid results?
w: Adding H2 to each C=C turns every 18-carbon oleic acid into stearic acid, so the product is tristearin, a solid fat. Hydrogenation does not break the ester bonds (that would be hydrolysis) or shorten the chains.

q: Cholesterol makes up about 25% of the lipid in some animal cell membranes. What is its main role there?
c: It fits between phospholipid tails and regulates membrane fluidity.
It forms channels that carry ions across the membrane.
It provides the polar head groups that face the water.
It is broken down in the membrane to supply energy.
h: Cholesterol is a rigid, mostly nonpolar steroid. Where in the bilayer would it sit, and what would it change?
w: Rigid cholesterol molecules slip between the fatty acid tails, keeping the membrane from becoming too fluid or too rigid. Ion channels are membrane proteins, and cholesterol is not used as a fuel.

q: When glycerol reacts with three fatty acids to make one triacylglycerol, how many ester bonds form and how many water molecules are released?
h: Esterification is a condensation: each –OH of glycerol joins one –COOH. What small molecule leaves each time?
w: Each of glycerol's three –OH groups condenses with one –COOH, forming one ester bond and losing one water each time: 3 ester bonds and 3 H2O.

q: Oleic acid, the main fatty acid in olive oil, is shown. How is it classified?
h: Count the C=C double bonds. For the omega number, count carbons from the CH<sub>3</sub> end (not the COOH end) to the first double-bond carbon.
w: There is one C=C, so it is monounsaturated. Counting from the methyl end, the double bond starts at carbon 9: omega-9. (For oleic acid the count from the COOH carbon, Δ9, happens to be 9 as well.) Omega-7 is a miscount, omega-6 needs two or more C=C, and a saturated acid has no C=C.

q: Linoleic acid, an essential fatty acid, is shown. What is its omega number?
h: Start counting at the CH<sub>3</sub> end of the chain. Stop at the first carbon of the first C=C you reach.
w: From the methyl carbon (carbon 1 on the omega scale), the first double bond begins at carbon 6, so linoleic acid is an omega-6 fatty acid. Omega-9 and omega-12 come from counting from the carboxyl end (Δ9 and Δ12).

q: α-Linolenic acid, found in flaxseed oil, is shown. Which description is correct?
c: Three cis double bonds; an omega-3 fatty acid
Three trans double bonds; an omega-3 fatty acid
Three cis double bonds; an omega-9 fatty acid
Two cis double bonds; an omega-6 fatty acid
h: Look at each C=C: are the two chain parts on the same side (cis) or opposite sides (trans)? Count the omega number from the CH<sub>3</sub> end.
w: All three C=C bonds have the chain continuing on the same side (cis), which puts kinks in the chain. The first double bond is at carbon 3 from the methyl end: omega-3. Omega-9 counts from the wrong end (Δ9).

q: The fatty acid shown forms during partial hydrogenation of vegetable oil. Which description is correct?
c: Trans; its nearly straight chain packs like a saturated fat
Cis; the C=C puts a sharp kink in the chain, so it packs poorly
Saturated; it has no C=C double bond, so it packs closely
Omega-3; the first C=C is three carbons from the CH<sub>3</sub> end
h: At the C=C, are the two chain parts on the same side or on opposite sides? Count the omega number from the CH<sub>3</sub> end.
w: The two chain parts leave the C=C on opposite sides (and so do the two H atoms), so this is a trans fatty acid (elaidic acid). Trans chains are nearly straight, pack closely like saturated chains, and raise LDL cholesterol. CH3(CH2)7CH= puts the C=C at carbon 9 from the methyl end: omega-9, not omega-3.

q: Oleic acid (shown) is completely hydrogenated with H<sub>2</sub> and a Ni catalyst. What is the product?
c: Elaidic acid, the trans isomer of oleic acid
Linoleic acid, with one more C=C double bond
h: Hydrogenation adds H<sub>2</sub> across each C=C. Does the number of carbons change?
w: H2 adds across the one C=C, giving the saturated 18-carbon acid stearic acid (C18H36O2), which melts higher; this is how oils become solid margarine. Trans isomers form only as a side product of partial hydrogenation; the carbon count does not change, and hydrogenation removes C=C bonds rather than adding them.

q: The triglyceride shown (in "MCT oil" supplements) is heated with NaOH (saponification). What are the products?
h: Saponification is ester hydrolysis in strong base. Each ester gives an alcohol and the salt of a carboxylic acid.
w: NaOH cleaves all three ester bonds: the alcohol part is glycerol and each acyl group becomes a carboxylate salt, 3 sodium octanoate (a soap). In base, the free acid is not left behind; it is deprotonated to the Na+ salt.

q: A triglyceride with the structure shown is most likely found as which, at room temperature?
c: A liquid oil: cis double bonds kink the chains, so they pack poorly
A solid fat: the double bonds make the chains straight and rigid
A solid fat: triglycerides with ester bonds are always solid
A liquid oil: it has no ester bonds to hold the molecules together
h: Look at the C=C bonds in each fatty acid chain. Straight chains pack tightly; kinked chains do not.
w: Each chain has a cis double bond, which bends it. Kinked chains cannot pack tightly, so the dispersion forces between molecules are weaker and the melting point is low: a liquid oil. Saturated (or trans) chains pack well, giving solid fats.

q: Glycerol (first structure) reacts with three molecules of the fatty acid shown (second structure). What forms?
c: A triglyceride with three ester bonds, plus 3 H<sub>2</sub>O
A triglyceride with three ether bonds, plus 3 H<sub>2</sub>O
A triglyceride with three ester bonds, plus 1 H<sub>2</sub>O
A phospholipid with three amide bonds, plus 3 H<sub>2</sub>O
h: Alcohol + carboxylic acid → ester + water. Glycerol has three –OH groups.
w: Each of glycerol's three –OH groups condenses with the –COOH of a fatty acid, forming one ester bond and releasing one H2O: 3 ester bonds and 3 H2O (esterification). Ethers and amides do not form from an acid and an alcohol.

q: Which lipid has the steroid ring system?
h: A steroid has four fused rings: three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring.
w: The correct structure is testosterone: four fused rings (6-6-6-5), the steroid nucleus. Retinol (vitamin A) has only one ring; the prostaglandin has one five-membered ring with two chains; the fatty acid has no ring.

q: The lipid shown is made in the liver and found in cell membranes. To which class of lipids does it belong?
h: Look at the ring system. Are there ester bonds or a phosphate anywhere?
w: The molecule (cholesterol) has four fused rings (three 6-membered, one 5-membered), the mark of a steroid. It has no ester bonds (triglyceride, wax) and no phosphate group (phospholipid).

q: Structures I and II are fatty acids with the same number of carbons. Which melts at the lower temperature, and why?
c: II; its cis double bond bends the chain, so molecules pack together poorly
I; its straight chain cannot pack closely with its neighbors
II; it has fewer carbon atoms, so its dispersion forces are weaker
I; a saturated chain has weaker dispersion forces than an unsaturated one
h: Both chains have 18 carbons. Look for a C=C and the kink it puts in the chain; kinks weaken packing between molecules.
w: Structure II (oleic acid) has a cis double bond that puts a kink in the chain; kinked chains cannot stack as closely, so the dispersion forces between molecules are weaker and the melting point is lower (oleic 13 °C vs stearic 70 °C). Both acids have 18 carbons, so chain length is not the reason.

q: Fish-oil supplements contain the fatty acid drawn below (EPA). Which classification is correct?
h: Count the C=C bonds, then count carbons from the methyl (omega) end to the FIRST double bond.
w: The chain has five C=C double bonds, so it is polyunsaturated. Counting from the CH3 (omega) end, the first double bond starts at carbon 3, so EPA is an omega-3 fatty acid. "Omega-5" comes from counting the number of double bonds instead of the position of the first one.

q: Structures I and II are both 18-carbon fatty acids with one double bond. Which statement about them is correct?
c: They are cis–trans isomers, and II has the higher melting point
They are cis–trans isomers, and I has the higher melting point
They are constitutional isomers, and II has the higher melting point
They are the same compound drawn in two different ways
h: Check the two groups on the double bond: same side or opposite sides? Straighter chains pack better and melt higher.
w: The chains are attached on the same side of the C=C in I (cis, oleic acid) and on opposite sides in II (trans, elaidic acid), so they are cis–trans isomers, not the same compound. The trans chain is nearly straight and packs like a saturated acid, so II has the higher melting point (45 °C vs 13 °C).

q: Pancreatic lipase breaks every ester bond in the triacylglycerol drawn below. What forms?
c: Glycerol plus three fatty acid molecules of two different kinds
Glycerol plus three identical fatty acid molecules
Glycerol plus three fatty acid molecules of three different kinds
A monoacylglycerol plus two identical fatty acid molecules
h: Lipase hydrolyzes every ester bond. Count the carbons in each acyl chain to see how many kinds of fatty acid there are.
w: All three ester bonds are hydrolyzed, giving glycerol and three fatty acids. Two of the chains have 4 carbons (butanoic acid) and one has 6 carbons (hexanoic acid), so there are two different fatty acids. Complete hydrolysis leaves no acyl group on the glycerol.

q: The triacylglycerol drawn below is treated with excess H<sub>2</sub> over a Ni catalyst until it is fully saturated. What amount of H<sub>2</sub> is consumed per mole of triacylglycerol?
h: One H<sub>2</sub> adds to each C=C. Count all the carbon–carbon double bonds in the three chains; ester C=O groups do not react.
w: The top chain has 1 C=C, the bottom chain has 2 and the chain on the middle carbon of glycerol (drawn to the left) is saturated: 1 + 2 + 0 = 3 mol H2. Counting the three C=O groups of the esters (6) is wrong; carbonyl groups are not hydrogenated under these conditions.

q: The membrane lipid shown is drawn with four labeled positions. In a cell-membrane bilayer, which labeled position lies in the nonpolar interior, away from water?
h: Phospholipids have a polar head (phosphate and charged group) and two nonpolar hydrocarbon tails. Which label is on a tail?
w: Position c is the end of a long hydrocarbon tail: nonpolar, so it points into the interior of the bilayer, away from water. Positions a (the choline group with its charged N+) and d (the charged phosphate) form the polar head that faces water; b is the glycerol backbone that joins head and tails.

q: Complete hydrolysis of the lipid shown gives which set of products?
c: Glycerol, two fatty acids, phosphate and choline
Sphingosine, one fatty acid, phosphate and choline
Glycerol, two fatty acids, phosphate and glucose
h: Find the backbone (three-carbon glycerol or sphingosine), count the acyl chains, and identify what is attached to the phosphate.
w: The three-carbon glycerol backbone carries two fatty acid esters and a phosphate that is also esterified to choline (the –CH2CH2N+(CH3)3 group). This is a glycerophospholipid (phosphatidylcholine). Three fatty acids would make it a triacylglycerol with no phosphate.

q: The ring system shown is found in cholesterol, estrogen, testosterone and cortisol. Which description fits it?
c: A steroid nucleus: three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring
A steroid nucleus: four six-membered rings
A steroid nucleus: two six-membered and two five-membered rings
A triacylglycerol core: three fatty acid chains on glycerol
h: Count the atoms in each fused ring. Steroids share one specific four-ring pattern.
w: Counting the corners of each fused ring gives 6, 6, 6 and 5: the steroid nucleus has three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring (17 carbons). Steroids are not built from fatty acids and glycerol, so they have no ester bonds and are not saponifiable.

q: Melting points of five fatty acids are listed. Which conclusion is supported by the table?
c: For a fixed chain length, each added cis double bond lowers the melting point
For saturated acids, a longer chain gives a lower melting point
Double bonds raise the melting point by strengthening dispersion forces
Melting point depends only on the number of carbons, not on double bonds
h: Compare the three 18-carbon acids with each other, then compare the three saturated acids with each other.
w: Among the 18-carbon acids, melting point drops from 70 °C (0 C=C) to 13 °C (1 cis C=C) to −5 °C (2 cis C=C): each cis double bond lowers the melting point because the kinks weaken packing. Among saturated acids, a longer chain melts higher (44 → 63 → 70 °C), so the second choice reverses the trend.

q: Four blood lipoproteins are described in the table (composition in % by mass). Which one is HDL, the "good cholesterol" that carries cholesterol back to the liver?
h: High-density lipoprotein is named for its density. Protein is denser than lipid, so the one richest in protein is densest.
w: HDL has the highest density and the highest protein content (about 50%), so it is IV: protein is denser than lipid, so more protein means a denser particle. Row III (25% protein, cholesterol-rich) is LDL, the "bad" cholesterol; row I, almost entirely lipid (triacylglycerol), is a chylomicron from the intestine; row II is VLDL.

q: The fatty acid composition of four dietary fats is shown. Which fat is most likely a liquid oil at room temperature?
h: Oils are rich in unsaturated fatty acids, whose cis double bonds keep the triacylglycerols from packing into a solid.
w: Fat II is only 14% saturated and 84% unsaturated (mostly monounsaturated), so its kinked chains pack poorly and it is a liquid: these are the numbers for olive oil. Fat IV (87% saturated, coconut oil) and fat I (63% saturated, butter) are solids; III (lard) is a soft solid.

q: The compound shown is made in the body from arachidonic acid, and aspirin works by blocking its synthesis. To which lipid class does it belong?
h: Count the carbons (20) and notice the five-membered ring in the middle of a fatty-acid-like chain.
w: A 20-carbon carboxylic acid with a five-membered ring and hydroxyl groups is a prostaglandin, one of the eicosanoids. Steroids have a four-ring nucleus with no carboxylic acid chain; sphingolipids contain an amide-linked fatty acid on sphingosine; waxes are simple esters of long-chain alcohols.

q: Lipids are grouped together as a class not by a shared functional group but by a shared property. Which property defines a lipid?
c: Insoluble in water but soluble in nonpolar solvents
Soluble in water because of many –OH groups
Made of repeating amino acid units
h: Fats, oils, waxes, steroids and phospholipids have very different structures. What do they all do in water?
w: A lipid is defined as a biomolecule that is insoluble in water and soluble in nonpolar solvents such as hexane or ether, because most of its structure is hydrocarbon. Carbohydrates are the water-soluble polyhydroxy compounds; only phospholipids contain phosphate, and proteins are the amino acid polymers.

q: Octanoic acid, a fatty acid in coconut and goat's milk fat, is drawn with four carbons lettered. Which letter marks the β carbon?
h: Greek letters start next to the carboxyl group: the carbon bonded to the –COOH carbon is α, the next one is β.
w: Counting from the carboxyl carbon (C1): the first carbon attached to it (b) is the α carbon (C2) and the next one, c, is the β carbon (C3), the carbon oxidized in β-oxidation. Letter a is the γ carbon (C4), and the far-end methyl carbon (d) is the omega (ω) carbon.

q: In the octanoic acid drawn, which lettered carbon is the omega (ω) carbon, the one used for naming omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acids?
h: Omega is the last letter of the Greek alphabet. Which carbon is farthest from the carboxyl group?
w: The omega carbon is the methyl carbon at the end of the chain farthest from –COOH, letter d. Counting from the carboxyl carbon, b is the α carbon (C2), c is the β carbon (C3) and a is the γ carbon (C4). In an omega-3 acid the first C=C begins three carbons in from carbon d.

q: Cholesterol is the starting material for several hormones. Which hormone is NOT made from cholesterol?
h: Steroid hormones keep the four-ring steroid nucleus of cholesterol. Which hormone is a protein instead?
w: Insulin is a small protein (51 amino acids) made in the pancreas, not a steroid. Testosterone, estradiol (sex hormones) and cortisol (an adrenal corticosteroid) are all steroids synthesized from cholesterol, as are aldosterone, bile salts and vitamin D.

q: Two students break down samples of the same vegetable oil (a triacylglycerol): one uses hot water with an H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> catalyst, the other uses aqueous NaOH. Compare the products of the two experiments.
c: Glycerol forms in each case; acid gives free fatty acids, NaOH gives fatty acid salts (soaps)
Acid gives glycerol and fatty acids; NaOH gives glycerol and three alcohols
Acid gives three esters; NaOH gives glycerol and fatty acids
Fatty acid salts form in each case; only NaOH releases glycerol
h: Both reactions break the same three ester bonds. Think about what a carboxylic acid becomes in a strongly basic solution.
w: Either way the three ester bonds are hydrolyzed and the alcohol portion, glycerol, is released. In acid the carboxylic acids are freed as RCOOH; in NaOH the base neutralizes them to RCOO−Na+, the salts we call soap. Fatty acids are the acid part of the ester, so they are never released as alcohols.

q: Phospholipids form the bilayer of cell membranes, but triacylglycerols do not; they collect as droplets inside fat cells. Why?
c: A triacylglycerol has no polar, charged head group, so it is nonpolar throughout
A triacylglycerol has only one fatty acid tail
Triacylglycerols are too water soluble to stay in a membrane
Triacylglycerols contain a steroid ring that is too rigid
h: A bilayer needs molecules with a polar head facing water and nonpolar tails facing inward. Compare the "head" of each lipid.
w: In a phospholipid one ester is replaced by a charged phosphate–amino alcohol head, so the molecule is amphipathic and lines up with heads toward water. In a triacylglycerol all three glycerol –OH groups are esterified to fatty acids, leaving no polar head; the whole molecule is nonpolar, so it simply clumps into oily droplets.

q: Four examples of substances crossing a cell membrane are described in the table. Which process is facilitated transport?
h: Facilitated transport uses a protein channel or carrier but no ATP, and moves the substance from high to low concentration.
w: Row II moves glucose down its concentration gradient through a carrier protein without ATP: facilitated transport. Rows I and IV are simple diffusion (small O2 and CO2 molecules slip directly through the bilayer), and row III is active transport (ATP is spent to pump K+ against its gradient).

q: A food company hydrogenates 2.0 mol of a cooking oil whose triacylglycerol contains one palmitic acid (16:0), one oleic acid (18:1) and one linoleic acid (18:2). What amount of H<sub>2</sub> is consumed, and how does the melting point change?
c: 2.0 mol H<sub>2</sub>; melting point is unchanged
h: Count the C=C bonds in one molecule (the number after the colon), then scale to 2.0 mol. Saturated chains pack better.
w: One molecule has 0 + 1 + 2 = 3 C=C bonds, so 1 mol of fat needs 3 mol H2 and 2.0 mol needs 6.0 mol H2. Removing the cis kinks lets the chains pack tightly, so the melting point rises (an oil becomes a solid fat). "3.0 mol" forgets the 2.0 mol of fat.
